title: On the Side of the Angel Insects
content: There’s one entomological accomplishment of which I’m proud, despite the fact that it has never had any discernible impact on my career or on the discipline of entomology in general. Almost 50 years ago, as part of Cornell University’s two‐week field ecology class held at the Archbold Biological Station in Florida during spring break in 1976, I found and collected a zorapteran—several zorapterans, actually. For non‐entomologist readers (and possibly for entomologist readers who have not yet taken their qualifying exams), the order Zoraptera was erected by Filippo Silvestri (1913) and has remained among the smallest and most enigmatic insect orders ever since. Inauspiciously, of the three species on which Silvestri based his recognition of the order more than a century ago (Zorotypus guineensis, Z. ceylonicus, and Z. javanicus), “none of these species have been described or observed again” as of 2024 (Kocarek and Kocarkova 2024). In fact, the “type material” for Zorotypus javanicus used by Silvestri in erecting the order went missing entirely and the species was described based on a juvenile female specimen, which perforce lacked genitalia (considered to be the gold standard material on which to base species descriptions throughout much of the history of insect systematics).
